The free plan now runs on credits: 300 per month, with a hard cap rather than automatic overage billing. Most results are third-party blogs, and none is Netlify's own pricing page, so check netlify.com/pricing before relying on these figures.

- **Allowance and cap:** Netlify's Free plan costs $0 and includes 300 credits per month. The Free plan uses a hard limit when the 300-credit balance is exhausted. Unused credits do not carry over to the next cycle.
- **Cost of deploys:** Production deployments consume 15 credits each. One blog estimates that 20 production deploys consume all 300 credits on deploys alone.
- **Other usage:** One guide gives an example in which a personal site that deploys 4 times a month (60 credits), serves 10 GB (200 credits) and gets 100,000 requests (20 credits) uses 280 credits and stays free.
- **Other features:** Free accounts get unlimited deploy previews, custom domains with SSL, functions, Netlify Database and Blob storage. Form submissions are listed as free and unlimited.
- **Exceeding limits:** One source says sites pausing if limits are exceeded until upgrade. Free accounts cannot buy extra credits; you must upgrade.
- **Legacy accounts:** Accounts created before September 4, 2025 reportedly stay on an older model: 100 GB bandwidth and 300 build minutes a month, both hard limits on the free tier.
- **Paid tiers for comparison:** Personal is $9 for 1,000 credits and Pro is $20 for 3,000 credits, with unlimited members on Pro.

The official GitHub Docs limits page confirms the 100 GB figure, but the snippets I retrieved don't show the 1 GB size limit directly. That figure appears only in secondary sources that quote the docs.

- **Bandwidth:** The official page lists a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month for Pages sites, with rate limits that may apply for service quality. GitHub Pages sites have a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month.
- **Site size:** A blog post quoting the limits page says published sites "may be no larger than 1 GB". Another source says GitHub Pages source repositories have a recommended limit of 1GB. I couldn't confirm this wording on the current official page.
- **Builds:** The official page sets a soft limit of 10 builds per hour, which does not apply to sites published with a custom GitHub Actions workflow. Deployments also time out after 10 minutes. GitHub Pages deployments will timeout if they take longer than 10 minutes.

Because the limits are soft, going over them usually doesn't cut off a site immediately. A third-party guide says that your site keeps working, but GitHub may throttle delivery during heavy load, and you might receive an email flagging the usage. Treat that as secondary commentary rather than official policy.

1	# F1b Live Check
2	
3	A tiny one-page site to test AI Studio end to end.
4	
5	This file is compiled from the global modules in `~/.ai-control/modules/`
6	(STRUCTURE, CODING, UX, WORKFLOW). Rebuild it with the `rebuild-claude-md` routine when the modules change.
7	Keep project-specific rules in the last section.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Structure
12	
13	### AI Control standard
14	Every project carries the standard scaffold:
15	- `.project` — the project marker, listing the `modules:` it uses, its `secrets:`, and `claude_md_generated`.
16	- `CLAUDE.md` — compiled from the global modules for this project.
17	- `.gitignore` — always covers `.env`.
18	- `.env` — this project's secrets (never committed).
19	- `updates/` — one folder per update (see below).
20	- `issues.txt` — running list of known issues and TODOs.
21	
22	### The updates/ folder
23	Each update is a folder named:
24	
25	```
26	updates/YYYY-MM-DD UPDATE_NAME - OPEN/      # while in progress
27	updates/YYYY-MM-DD UPDATE_NAME - CLOSED/     # when done
28	```
29	
30	Inside each update folder:
31	- **`update vX.md`** — the version-X plan (`X` starts at 1). Contains the goal, the phased roadmap to reach it, and live status tracking: what's done, what decisions were made, what's next. Bump to `v2`, `v3`… when the plan is substantially reworked.
32	- **`wiki.md`** — the decisions and lessons this update taught us: principles, what works and what doesn't. This is durable knowledge, not status.
33	- **Optional extra files** — logs for anything else related to the update, and any research-spike code that ran in isolation (see WORKFLOW.md). An update can be reopened (flip `CLOSED` → `OPEN`) to finish or fix something.
34	
35	### Per-ecosystem conventions
36	- **Follow each ecosystem's own norms** — `src/`, `tests/`, the standard layout for whatever stack the project uses. Don't impose a foreign structure on it.
37	- Keep small projects **flat and simple**; add folders only when the project genuinely grows into them. Avoid premature nesting.
38	- **Rust/Tauri:** build output goes to the **shared Cargo target** (`~/.cargo-shared-target`, set globally in `~/.cargo/config.toml`), not a per-project `target/`. A missing local `target/` is expected; the first build after a clean is a full rebuild. Never add a per-project `target-dir`/`CARGO_TARGET_DIR` override. Full details: `wiki/shared-cargo-target.md`.
39	
40	### Modular by default
41	- Structure code so any piece can be understood and fixed **in isolation**, with its own bounded context. Clear module boundaries, minimal cross-coupling. See CODING.md for how this shapes the code itself and UX.md for how it shapes the UI.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Coding
46	
47	### Modularize for isolated context
48	- Write code so any part can be picked up, understood, and fixed **on its own**, without loading the whole system into your head. That's the point of modularity here: an isolated context to work in and an isolated thing to change.
49	- Draw clear module boundaries with small, explicit interfaces. Keep cross-module coupling low so a change stays contained and a bug has one obvious home.
50	
51	### Keep it minimal
52	- Build **only what's truly needed**. Don't add abstraction, configuration, or layers on speculation — add them when a real need shows up.
53	- Prefer reuse over duplication: shared helpers and components over copy-paste, but don't over-generalize before there's a second real caller.
54	
55	### Test what matters
56	- Cover core logic, risky paths, and anything that would silently regress. Skip tests for trivial glue.
57	- Phases in a roadmap mostly end with tests that lock in what they built (see WORKFLOW.md) — this is how we keep moving without breaking earlier work.
58	
59	### Idiomatic to the ecosystem
60	- Match the conventions, naming, and idioms of whatever stack and surrounding code the project uses. Read the neighbors before writing; new code should look like it belongs.
61	- Follow each ecosystem's standard tooling for formatting, linting, and layout rather than inventing house style.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## UX
66	
67	### Always bring in UX experts
68	- For anything with a user-facing surface, **always launch a dedicated UX expert agent** to think the experience through before and during the build.
69	- For a surface with multiple parts, **launch several UX experts in parallel**, each owning a part, so the whole experience is deeply considered rather than improvised. Act as the orchestrator (see WORKFLOW.md) and synthesize their thinking.
70	
71	### Cut everything unnecessary
72	- Approach every UI as Steve Jobs would: **relentlessly remove anything that isn't truly needed.** The default answer to a new element, option, or screen is "does this earn its place?" — if not, it's gone.
73	- Minimal by conviction: the fewest screens, controls, and steps that do the job well.
74	
75	### Minimal visual system
76	- Keep the **number of fonts to a minimum** — ideally one or two, used consistently. Same discipline for colors, spacing, and sizes: a small, deliberate scale, not ad-hoc values.
77	- Aim for a polished, modern result. When the stack supports it, lean on solid component foundations (e.g. Tailwind / shadcn-style primitives) rather than hand-rolling one-off styles.
78	
79	### Standardized, reusable, isolated components
80	- Build the UI from **reusable, standardized components** — define a thing once and reuse it everywhere, so the interface stays consistent and cheap to change.
81	- Keep components **highly isolated**: each stands on its own with a clear interface, so it can be understood, restyled, or fixed without touching the rest. This mirrors the modularity rule in CODING.md and STRUCTURE.md.
82	
83	### Fundamentals
84	- Responsive across the sizes the project targets, and accessible by default — real contrast, keyboard reachability, sensible focus, meaningful labels.
85	- Sensible defaults, fast feedback, and clear, honest error states over decoration.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Workflow
90	
91	### Commit and backup
92	- **Always commit AND push after every change.** No change is ever left uncommitted or unpushed. Each working change is its own commit — small, focused, one logical unit per commit — and is pushed to the remote immediately. Don't batch unrelated edits.
93	- **Everything lives on GitHub.** Every project has a GitHub remote and every commit is pushed right away; nothing important stays local-only. If a project isn't backed up yet, fix that first.
94	- Write plain, honest commit messages that say what changed and why. Never commit secrets — `.env` stays in `.gitignore`.
95	
96	### Roadmaps and phases
97	- Any non-trivial update or coding task starts with a **roadmap broken into phases**. Design the phases before writing code and record them in the update's `update vX.md` (see STRUCTURE.md for the updates layout).
98	- **Most phases end with tests** that lock in what that phase built, so we don't break earlier work as we go. Test what matters — core logic, risky paths, anything that would silently regress — not trivial glue.
99	- Track status as you go: what's done, what decisions were made, what's next. Keep `update vX.md` current.
100	
101	### Research spikes
102	- When a phase involves a new API, an unfamiliar library, or a genuinely new design, make it a **research phase**: a throwaway spike that runs *outside the main code*, inside the update folder, in an isolated environment.
103	- Use the spike to find out what actually works before committing the main codebase to an approach. Capture the findings — principles, what worked, what didn't — in the update's `wiki.md`.
104	
105	### Act as an orchestrator
106	- Prefer to **delegate to your own agents** rather than doing everything inline. Act as the orchestrator: decompose the work, fan out to focused agents, and synthesize.
107	- For anything with a UX dimension, **always launch a UX expert agent** — and launch several in parallel for different parts of the surface so the experience is thoroughly thought through. See UX.md.
108	
109	### Verify before moving on
110	- Verify changes by running the actual thing, not just by trusting a green test. Confirm the phase does what it set out to do before you commit and move to the next.
111	
112	---
113	
114	## Project-specific rules

content.content:
**Site size**
- Published sites are capped at 1 GB.
- Source repositories have a recommended limit of 1 GB.

**Bandwidth**
- There is a soft limit of 100 GB per month. It isn't strictly enforced.

**Builds and deployments**
- There is a soft limit of 10 builds per hour. "This limit does not apply if you build and publish your site with a custom GitHub Actions workflow."
- Deployments time out if they run longer than 10 minutes.

**Other limits**
- You can create only one user or organization site per account.
- Rate limits may apply. Requests that trigger them receive HTTP status 429.
- Sites over quota may not be served, or GitHub Support may contact you about reducing your impact.

**Prohibited commercial uses**
- GitHub Pages "is not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web-hosting service" to run a business, e-commerce site, or commercial SaaS.
- Sites shouldn't handle sensitive transactions, such as sending passwords or credit card numbers.
- The GitHub Terms of Service also apply, including restrictions on get-rich-quick schemes, sexually obscene content, and violent or threatening content.
- Educational copies of existing websites are allowed if you write the code yourself, the site collects no user data, and it has a prominent disclaimer stating it is unaffiliated with the original and made for educational purposes.

**Private repository or plan requirements**
- The page doesn't mention these, so this content can't answer that question.

input.prompt: Is HTTPS automatic for github.io and custom domains? Any availability note about GitHub Free public repos vs private repos on paid plans?

toolu_01QwNC6CaWWDnRxvc8xURQmR.prompt: Is HTTPS automatic for github.io and custom domains? Any availability note about GitHub Free public repos vs private repos on paid plans?

content.content:
**Automatic HTTPS:**
- **github.io domains:** Sites created after June 15, 2016 are served over HTTPS automatically.
- **Custom domains:** The page says sites with correctly configured custom domains "support HTTPS and HTTPS enforcement." Enforcement isn't automatic, though. A repository admin must select **Enforce HTTPS** in the Pages settings. GitHub also has to provision a certificate, which can take several minutes, and DNS problems can prevent it.

**Plan availability:** The page doesn't say whether HTTPS differs between GitHub Free and paid plans, or between public and private repositories. The only plan reference is in the warning that a Pages site can be publicly available even when its repository is private, "if your plan or organization allows it." That note concerns site visibility, not HTTPS.

input.title: GitHub Pages vs Netlify for our one-page site
input.question: Research: compare two free ways to host this static page (GitHub Pages vs Netlify) and write up which fits us better.
input.summary: Pick GitHub Pages. Our rules already require every project to live on GitHub, so a git push publishes the page. It needs no extra account and has no usage credits to run out. Netlify's free plan works too, but it charges credits for each deploy and stops at a hard cap.
input.body:
## The answer
**Use GitHub Pages.** Our page is a single file (`hello.html`) with no build step. Our project rules already say every project must have a GitHub remote and push every commit. With GitHub Pages, that push is also the publish step: no second account, no second dashboard and no meter to watch. Netlify is a good service, but its extra features (deploy previews, forms, functions) don't help a one-page site, and its new credit-based free plan adds a catch we don't need.

## Side-by-side

| | **GitHub Pages** | **Netlify (Free)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | Free | Free ($0 plan) |
| **Setup** | Push the repo to GitHub, then Settings → Pages → choose a branch. About 2 minutes. | Make a Netlify account, connect the GitHub repo (or drag and drop the folder). About 5 minutes. |
| **How updates go live** | `git push` and the site updates in about a minute | `git push` and Netlify redeploys automatically |
| **Free-plan limits** | 1 GB site size. Soft limit of 100 GB/month bandwidth. Soft limit of 10 builds/hour. | 300 credits/month with a hard cap. A production deploy costs **15 credits**, bandwidth 20 credits/GB, requests 2 credits per 10k. |
| **What happens at the limit** | Soft limits: GitHub may throttle the site or email you. It is rarely an issue for small sites. | Hard cap: the free plan can't buy extra credits, so you upgrade or the site is paused. |
| **Free address** | `username.github.io/repo` | `name.netlify.app` |
| **Custom domain** | Yes, free | Yes, free |
| **HTTPS** | Automatic on github.io. On a custom domain, the certificate is issued automatically; you tick "Enforce HTTPS" once. | Automatic, including on custom domains |
| **Extras** | None, just static hosting | Deploy previews, forms, serverless functions, redirects and headers |
| **Commercial use** | Not allowed for running a business, online shop or SaaS | Allowed |

## Catches to know
**GitHub Pages**
- On a free GitHub account, the repo generally has to be **public** to use Pages. Publishing from a private repo needs a paid plan. Our page is meant to be public anyway.
- It isn't allowed as free hosting for a business or online shop. That doesn't apply to a test page.
- You only get custom headers or server-side redirects if you put a CDN in front of the site. We don't need them.

**Netlify**
- New free accounts (since Sept 2025) are on **credits**. About 20 production deploys in a month use up the whole 300-credit allowance, even with zero visitors. Because we commit and push after every change, deploying on every push could hit that cap. Turning off auto-deploy, or deploying only some branches, would avoid it, but that's one more thing to manage.
- It's another account and dashboard to manage, outside GitHub.

## Why GitHub Pages fits us
1. **It matches our existing workflow.** Our rules make GitHub the home of every project, so publishing is just the push we already do.
2. **There's nothing to run out.** Soft limits far above what a one-page site uses, versus a deploy-counting hard cap.
3. **It's the minimal option.** One service instead of two, in line with our "only what's needed" rule.
4. **HTTPS and a custom domain are free on both,** so Netlify has no advantage there.

**When to revisit:** if the site later needs forms, server functions, preview links for each change, or commercial use, Netlify (or a similar host) becomes the better fit.

## Next step (for the director)
This project **has no GitHub remote yet** (`git remote -v` is empty). The first step is to create the GitHub repo and push, which our workflow rules require anyway. After that, turn on Pages for the `main` branch, root folder. Note that the page lives at `/hello.html` unless it is renamed to or linked from `index.html`.

*Limits were checked in Nov 2026. Netlify's credit figures come from its pricing page, and the hard-cap and pausing details come from third-party write-ups. Re-check both before relying on them.*
